articles.title: Night owls may face a higher risk of acquired premature ejaculation
articles.summary: Men who naturally prefer staying up late might face a higher risk of developing premature ejaculation. A new study links this biological sleep preference and symptom severity to daily lifestyle routines and psychological stress.

articles.title: Your gut may help your brain decide what to remember
articles.summary: Signals traveling from the gut to the brain may help turn meals into lasting memories. Rats showed stronger memory activity after consuming nutritious foods, but not after drinking sweet liquids with little or no nutritional value. Blocking the vagus nerve erased this effect and made it harder for the animals to remember where food had been located. Over time, diets high in fat and sugar also weakened this memory system.

articles.title: Losing an election is associated with lower social trust among polarized voters
articles.summary: A new study suggests that voters whose preferred party loses a national election experience a decline in generalized social trust. This gap widens among highly polarized voters who harbor strong negative feelings toward opposing political parties.

articles.title: Eating within 8 hours may help keep the aging brain sharp
articles.summary: Eating within a shorter daily window may help protect certain thinking skills as people age. In a small six-month trial, older women who limited eating to about 8 to 9 hours a day performed better on planning and problem-solving tests than those who ate over 12 hours. Both groups lost similar amounts of weight, hinting that when people eat could matter in addition to how much they eat.

articles.title: A hidden Alzheimer’s tipping point may decide who gets dementia
articles.summary: Scientists have identified a possible tipping point that helps determine whether Alzheimer’s-related brain changes lead to dementia. The key may lie in how the brain’s immune cells respond to plaques and tau, offering a promising new target for treatments designed to extend cognitive resilience.

articles.title: Inside the Backrooms: The internet’s creepiest place is becoming a tourist attraction
articles.summary: The Backrooms began as a single eerie image of empty yellow rooms, but internet users transformed it into a vast fictional world that feels disturbingly real. Through videos, games, maps, survival guides and social media stories, audiences do more than watch the horror unfold. They help build and explore it. Researchers suggest this popularity reflects a new kind of digital tourism, where people emotionally enter imaginary places filled with mystery, nostalgia and unease.

articles.title: How a child’s brain processes emotional faces offers a surprising glimpse into their future friendships
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that a child’s early brain activity can forecast their future social life. Surprisingly, the same neural response to emotional faces predicts very different patterns of peer engagement for boys and girls entering adolescence.
